description: Hardwoods, softwoods and manufactured boards — properties, defects and timber finishes.
content_html:
Timber in Design and Industry

Timber is one of the most versatile structural materials available to designers, and the most popular choice for the in-depth extended response question in the written exam. Understanding the difference between hardwoods, softwoods and manufactured boards—and knowing named examples of each—is essential. The distinction begins at the tree: hardwoods come from deciduous trees (broad-leaved, generally slow-growing), while softwoods come from coniferous trees (evergreen, needle-leaved, generally faster-growing).

Importantly, “hardwood” and “softwood” are botanical classifications, not descriptions of physical hardness. Balsa—which is famously soft to the touch—is technically a hardwood because it comes from a deciduous tree. Conversely, some conifers produce surprisingly dense timber.

Key Fact

Hardwoods come from deciduous (broad-leaved) trees; softwoods come from coniferous (needle-leaved) trees. The terms describe botanical classification, not physical hardness. Balsa is a hardwood despite being soft; some conifers produce dense timber.

Named Hardwoods

The following hardwoods are named in the specification and are likely to appear in exam questions:

  • Oak—a dense, strong hardwood with an attractive grain and excellent durability. Used in furniture, flooring, wine barrels and construction. Oak can be finished naturally or stained; it reacts with iron fixings (producing dark stains), so stainless or brass fixings are preferred.
  • Beech—a pale, fine-grained hardwood that is very hard and resistant to splitting. Commonly used in furniture (especially chair seats and legs), tool handles and children’s toys. Beech machines and sands very cleanly.
  • Mahogany—a medium-density tropical hardwood with a rich reddish-brown colour and an interlocking grain that resists warping. Traditional choice for furniture, interior joinery and boat building. Sustainability concerns exist around tropical hardwood sourcing; look for FSC-certified stock.
  • Balsa—extremely low density (as low as 100–200 kg/m³), making it the lightest commercial timber. Used for model making and structural cores in composite panels (e.g. wind turbine blades). Despite its softness, it has a high strength-to-weight ratio.
  • Jelutong—a fine-grained, uniform hardwood widely used in D&T education for model making and pattern carving. It is easy to cut, sand and shape accurately, making it ideal for producing prototypes and moulding patterns.

Named Softwoods

  • Scots pine—a widely available European softwood used for structural timber, joinery and furniture. It has a pale yellow colour with distinct resin pockets. Moderately strong and easy to work.
  • Western red cedar—a naturally durable softwood with high rot resistance due to its phenolic oils. Used for exterior cladding, garden furniture and roof shingles without needing chemical treatment. Has a distinctive reddish-brown colour and pleasant aroma.
  • Parana pine—a fine-grained softwood from South America, unusual in softwoods for being relatively knot-free. Used in high-quality interior joinery, staircases and shelving where a clean appearance is needed. Its limited availability has made it more expensive than other softwoods.
Key Fact

Western red cedar’s natural durability comes from its phenolic oils, not a chemical preservative treatment—making it an environmentally preferred choice for exterior use. Jelutong is the standard studio modelling timber in D&T because it machines and carves accurately.

Manufactured Boards

Manufactured boards are engineered sheet materials. They eliminate many of the defects of solid timber and are available in large, consistent sheets (typically 2440 × 1220 mm). Key types:

  • Plywood—layers of veneer bonded with adjacent grains at 90° to each other. This cross-grain construction gives high strength in all directions and resistance to splitting. Structural grades (e.g. WBP—water and boil proof) are used in construction; decorative grades use hardwood face veneers.
  • MDF (medium-density fibreboard)—fine wood fibres bonded with synthetic resin under heat and pressure. Produces a uniform, smooth surface with no grain, which takes paint and veneers extremely well. However, MDF is heavy, absorbs moisture at edges and cannot be used structurally where loads must be resisted.
  • Chipboard (particleboard)—compressed wood chips bonded with adhesive. Cheaper than MDF or plywood; commonly used in flat-pack furniture (often surfaced with a melamine laminate). Weak at the edges and screws do not hold as well as in solid timber.
  • Hardboard—a thin, dense sheet made from wood pulp fibres compressed under steam and heat. One face is smooth, the other textured. Used for drawer bases, backs of furniture and low-cost panels.

Natural timber contains inherent defects that affect quality and strength. Common defects include:

  • Knots—where branches once grew. Knots disrupt the grain, weaken the timber at that point and can shrink and fall out over time. Structural timber grades limit knot size and position.
  • Shrinkage and warping—timber continues to absorb and release moisture after felling. Uneven drying causes cupping (edges curl up), bowing (along the length) and twisting. Kiln-drying reduces but does not eliminate movement.
  • Shakes—cracks that run along the grain. Ring shakes follow the annual growth rings; star shakes radiate outward from the centre. Both weaken the board and may open further as the timber dries.
  • Fungal attack—wet rot and dry rot fungi degrade wood fibres if timber remains damp. Preservative treatment (e.g. pressure impregnation with copper-based compounds) is used for outdoor structural timber.

Manufactured boards overcome most of these defects because the manufacturing process eliminates directional grain dependence, large knots and growth-related stresses. This is a key advantage when selecting sheet material for flat furniture components.

Finishing timber protects it from moisture, UV light and physical wear, and enhances appearance. Common finishes include:

  • Varnish—a clear resin coating that cures to a hard, durable surface. Polyurethane varnish is water-resistant and tough, suitable for floors and furniture. Satin and gloss sheens are available.
  • Stain—penetrates the timber fibres to change colour without hiding grain. Oil-based stains are absorbed deeply; water-based stains raise the grain slightly but have lower VOC emissions.
  • Paint—fully opaque finish that hides grain. Requires a primer coat on bare wood to seal the surface and improve adhesion. Suitable for MDF (which does not have a visible grain) and exterior joinery.
  • Danish oil / linseed oil—penetrating oils that soak into the wood fibres, feeding the timber and giving a natural, low-sheen appearance. Often used on hardwoods where the grain is intended to be visible. Requires periodic reapplication.
exam_tip_html: Timbers and boards is consistently the most popular choice for Question 6, and the exam mark scheme rewards depth rather than breadth. Use specific names: “oak” not “hardwood”; “plywood” not “manufactured board”. Link each property to a product application: for example, “beech is used for chair seats because its hardness and fine grain resist scratching and machine cleanly for an accurate fit.” Include at least one manufactured board in your response to show range. For questions on defects, name the defect (knot, shake, fungal attack) rather than writing vaguely about ‘imperfections’. Sustainability answers must be specific: “FSC-certified mahogany ensures timber is sourced from sustainably managed forests” beats “use sustainable wood.”
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Hardwoods come from deciduous trees (oak, beech, mahogany, balsa, jelutong); softwoods from coniferous trees (Scots pine, western red cedar, parana pine). The terms describe tree type, not physical hardness.
  • Manufactured boards (plywood, MDF, chipboard, hardboard) overcome natural timber defects such as knots, shakes and warping by bonding fibres or veneers into consistent sheets.
  • Timber finishes (varnish, stain, paint, oil) protect against moisture and UV damage. Western red cedar’s natural phenolic oils mean it resists rot without chemical treatment—a key exam point on sustainability.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is a hardwood?
A) Scots pine
B) Western red cedar
C) Parana pine
D) Mahogany
Name the timber defect that occurs when cracks run along the grain following the annual growth rings.
practice_questions.marks: Ring shake [2 marks]. (Accept: shake [1 mark] with no specification of type.)

practice_questions.text: Describe two ways in which MDF differs from solid timber that make it suitable for painted furniture components.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 3 marks from:
• MDF has a uniform, grain-free surface that takes paint smoothly without visible grain showing through [1]
• MDF does not warp, cup or twist as solid timber can when moisture levels change [1]
• MDF is produced in large, consistent sheet sizes (typically 2440 × 1220 mm) with no knots or natural defects [1]
• MDF can be cut and routed to precise profiles and edges without splitting [1]
(1 mark per valid point; max 3)

practice_questions.text: Explain why jelutong is preferred over oak for producing prototype models in a design studio.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks from:
• Jelutong is a fine, uniform-grained timber [1] that can be cut, carved and sanded to precise shapes accurately [1]
• Oak is a dense, hard timber [1] that requires more effort and specialist tools to work accurately at small model scales [1]
• Jelutong takes adhesives cleanly and can be painted or primed easily for presentation [1]
• Oak’s coarse grain would show through paint finishes on fine-detail models [1]
(2 marks per developed comparative point; max 4)

practice_questions.text: A furniture manufacturer is designing a garden bench to be sold without surface treatment. Explain, with reference to the material’s properties, why western red cedar is a more suitable timber choice than Scots pine for this application.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies western red cedar’s phenolic oils as the source of its natural rot resistance, explains how this removes the need for chemical preservative treatment (cost and environmental benefit), compares Scots pine’s need for pressure treatment to withstand outdoor conditions, and links the material properties directly to the product context (untreated garden bench).
Secure: Explains that cedar is naturally rot-resistant and pine needs treatment for outdoor use, with some material-property detail.
Developing: States cedar is more durable outdoors without explaining the mechanism or product context sufficiently.
Emerging: Vague statement that cedar is ‘better for outside’ with no property-based reasoning.

practice_questions.text: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of using plywood rather than solid oak for the seat and back panels of a dining chair. Consider structural performance, aesthetics, cost and sustainability.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Balanced discussion with developed points on both sides across multiple criteria. Advantages of plywood: consistent dimensions with no warping risk; cross-grain lamination gives strength in multiple directions; can be bent into curved profiles using steam or formers; typically cheaper per board metre than solid oak; can use thin oak face veneer for aesthetic appearance. Disadvantages: edge appearance is unattractive unless lipped; structural grades have visible layers; cannot be re-surfaced by sanding as many times as solid oak; relies on adhesives whose performance degrades. Reaches a reasoned judgement about which set of factors weighs more heavily for the dining chair context.
Secure: Two or more developed points on each side with some product-relevant detail; judgement present.
Developing: Points on both sides identified but limited development; judgement weak.
Emerging: Mainly one side addressed or points superficial.

knowledge_checks.q: Why is balsa classified as a hardwood despite being very soft to the touch?
options: It comes from a deciduous, broad-leaved tree
It has a very high tensile strength
It is harvested from coniferous trees

knowledge_checks.q: Which manufactured board is made by bonding alternate layers of veneer with grains at 90° to each other?
Western red cedar resists rot without chemical treatment because of its natural _____.
Match each timber to its key characteristic:
right: Fine-grained, easy to carve — preferred for model making
Rich reddish-brown colour, resists warping — used in furniture
Very hard and fine-grained — used for chair seats and tool handles

flashcard_questions.q: What type of trees do hardwoods come from?
What type of trees do softwoods come from?
Which hardwood is preferred in D&T studios for model making because it carves and machines accurately?
Why does western red cedar resist rot outdoors without chemical treatment?
flashcard_questions.a: Its natural phenolic oils repel moisture and decay.

flashcard_questions.q: Oak reacts with iron fixings — what finish does this produce?
flashcard_questions.a: Dark stains; use stainless or brass fixings instead.

flashcard_questions.q: What construction method gives plywood its strength in multiple directions?
flashcard_questions.a: Alternating veneer layers with grains at 90° to each other.

flashcard_questions.q: Which manufactured board has a smooth, grain-free surface ideal for painting?
What timber defect occurs when a branch insertion disrupts the grain and weakens the board?
What type of timber defect follows the annual growth rings as a crack?
Parana pine is unusual among softwoods for being virtually _____ free.
Which hardwood has a very low density (as low as 100–200 kg/m³) and is used in model making?
What does FSC certification guarantee when purchasing mahogany?
flashcard_questions.a: The timber comes from a sustainably managed forest.

flashcard_questions.q: Danish oil is described as a penetrating finish — what does it do to the timber?
flashcard_questions.a: It soaks into the fibres to feed the wood and give a natural low-sheen appearance.

glossary_terms.definition: Broad-leaved trees that shed their leaves seasonally and typically produce denser, harder timber.
Evergreen, needle-leaved trees such as pine and cedar, which grow faster than deciduous trees and produce less dense timber.
Sheet materials made by bonding wood fibres, particles or veneers together with adhesives, to overcome the natural defects of solid timber.
